headline: An AI-spending scare handed stocks their worst day since June and pulled the 10-year down to 4.94%, even as two Fed officials called for more hikes.
dateline: Monday, November 2, 2026 · closes as of Fri Oct 30

rundown.h: Two Fed presidents say more hikes are coming.
rundown.p: Two days after the Fed held at 3.75–4.00%, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said the committee needs at least two more quarter-point hikes and that policy sits at least 50 basis points below modestly restrictive. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said more firming will be needed soon. Logan added that skipping a meeting doesn't change where rates are headed.

rundown.h: Tuesday's midterms could reshuffle the policy outlook.
rundown.p: Democrats are widely expected to win the House in Tuesday's midterms, while control of the Senate looks less certain, Reuters reports. Strategists say a Democratic sweep could bring more scrutiny of AI, data centers, big banks and crypto. The result also shapes the outlook for spending, tariffs and energy policy heading into 2027.

rundown.h: Refining windfalls carried Exxon and Chevron past forecasts.
rundown.p: Exxon earned $4.23 a share adjusted, beating the $4.08 expected, and plans $20 billion of buybacks in 2027. Chevron's adjusted $5.28 topped about $4.89, as downstream earnings more than quadrupled to $4.9 billion and net debt fell $7.8 billion. Fat refining margins did the work, not crude prices, which tells you where the oil shock is paying out.

rundown.h: Apple kicks off a busy week as profits run hot.
rundown.p: Apple reports today, with AMD, Qualcomm and Palantir among more than 100 S&P 500 companies due this week, per Reuters. About half the index has reported, and third-quarter earnings are on pace to rise 31% from a year ago, per LSEG. The S&P still finished October up about 1% and is up more than 10% for the year.

rundown.h: Bonds just had their best month in nearly three years.
rundown.p: The 10-year Treasury yield fell about 36 basis points in October, its biggest monthly drop since December 2023, after topping 5.30% earlier in the month, per Trading Economics and Reuters. Investors piled into bonds as tech stocks slid. It is the first real relief for borrowers this fall, but hawkish Fed talk could cut it short.

dive.title: Uncle Sam's $2 trillion year, and the interest bill is driving
dive.dek: Washington's FY2026 deficit was the biggest in five years, and interest on the debt now costs more than the military.
dive.body:
The government's fiscal year ended Sept. 30, and the final tally is in. Treasury's year-end statement, released Oct. 16, put the FY2026 deficit at $1.992 trillion, up $217 billion, or 12%, from $1.775 trillion in FY2025 and the largest gap in five years. The American Action Forum's breakdown (Oct. 18) puts it at 6.1% of GDP, about $140 billion worse than CBO had projected. And there was no recession to blame.

Interest is where the money went. Net interest reached $1.1 trillion, about 19% of all federal revenue and more than the $965 billion spent on national defense. Gross interest set a record at $1.36 trillion, up $144 billion. Revenue rose 3% to $5.4 trillion, but corporate taxes fell 16% to $381 billion, and customs duties slipped 11% to $173 billion because Treasury paid back about $130 billion of IEEPA tariffs after the Supreme Court struck them down. In September alone, refunds swallowed $19.4 billion of the $25.3 billion collected at the border.

Why it matters: debt held by the public is now $32.4 trillion, about 100% of GDP. With the 10-year near 5% and a December hike likely, every cheap note that matures gets rolled at a higher rate, which makes next year's interest bill bigger still. Treasury supply sets the floor for everyone else's borrowing costs. If you're underwriting a warehouse cap rate or an outdoor-storage refinancing, that floor is the 10-year.

What would change the picture: this week's refunding. In August, Treasury said it would keep note and bond auction sizes unchanged "for at least the next several quarters" (the 10-year auction was $42 billion). Any hint of bigger auctions would push long yields up; leaning harder on short-term bills would keep the pressure at the front end. A Fed that stops hiking would ease the interest bill. Oil above $100 keeping inflation sticky would do the opposite.

items.title: Q3 employment costs rose 0.8%, in line, as benefits outpaced wages

chart.t: ECI, civilian total compensation, % change from a year earlier
chart.src: Source: BLS via FRED (ECIALLCIV, seasonally adjusted index); year-over-year changes computed from the index.

items.body:
The employment cost index rose 0.8% in the third quarter, released Friday, matching the 0.8% consensus and down from 0.9% in the second quarter. Wages and salaries rose 0.7% after 0.9%, while benefits rose 0.9% after 1.0%. Over 12 months, total compensation was up 3.4%, unchanged; wages slowed to 3.1% from 3.2% and benefits picked up to 3.9% from 3.8%.

The detail split two ways. Private-industry health benefit costs rose 6.4% from a year earlier, up from 6.0%. State and local government compensation cooled to 0.6% from 1.0%. After inflation, private-sector wages and salaries fell 0.6% over the year. Annual compensation growth has eased from a 5.1% peak in 2022 and has held at 3.4% for four quarters.

Markets barely reacted to the in-line print; a tech selloff drove Friday's trade. The 10-year yield slid to about 4.9%, a seven-week low, and CME FedWatch odds of a December hike eased to roughly 72–76% from about 85% after Wednesday's decision.

experts.who: Priscilla Thiagamoorthy, senior economist, BMO Capital Markets
experts.view: Labor-cost inflation keeps moving in the right direction for the Fed.

experts.who: Matthew Martin, senior U.S. economist, Oxford Economics
experts.view: Health insurance costs are climbing at their fastest pace since 2005, a pressure point inside the benefits line.
Labor cost pressure looks relatively contained, but benefits are outrunning wages and pay isn't keeping up with prices.

items.lean: Thiagamoorthy and Dellamotta read wage pressure as contained; Martin flags rising health costs.

lead.title: Trump gives Iran talks more time, and oil gives back some of its war premium
lead.body:
Washington is giving talks more room before the midterms. Secretary of State Rubio said Saturday that no decision had been made on renewed strikes and that President Trump prefers a diplomatic outcome, and Axios reported Trump told Prime Minister Netanyahu he wants to give diplomacy more time. At an Iowa rally Sunday, Trump said the war would end one way or the other.

Tehran is still at the table. Foreign Minister Araqchi called talks with Qatari mediators ongoing and progressing; on Monday an official said Iran's negotiators had left the session but a draft is circulating and another meeting is possible. The shipping lanes haven't calmed: an LNG tanker was attacked Friday and UKMTO said a ship was hit by a projectile in Hormuz on Sunday.
lead.reach: Through oil and shipping. Brent fell $4.79, or 4.2%, to $108.64 by 10:20 GMT Monday and WTI slid to $99.71, after Brent rose about 15% in October to a six-month high.

views.view: The new month brought fresh hope of a breakthrough in the Iran stalemate, and that hope is what's pulling prices lower.
Record freight costs, tight tanker capacity and recovering Chinese imports should keep prices high, with Brent near $110 at the end of 2026.

reading.title: The Tiger who walked away
reading.dek: In March 2000, one of the best hedge fund managers of his era decided being early was too expensive and handed his investors their money back.
reading.body:
Picture spring 2000. Tech stocks are flying, your dentist has a hot tip on an internet company with no revenue, and one of the best money managers alive is... giving the money back. On March 30, 2000, Julian Robertson wrote to his limited partners that Tiger Management was done and every dollar of outside capital would be returned.

This was not a man short on credentials. A Salisbury, North Carolina native who learned the business as a stockbroker at Kidder, Peabody, Robertson opened Tiger in May 1980 with $8.8 million. For the next 18 years it compounded at 31.7% a year after fees, versus roughly 12.7% for the S&P 500, and swelled past $20 billion. The recipe was almost boring: judge stocks on earnings and price, then outwork everyone on research. Tiger posted losing years in only four of its 21 years, the kind of consistency that turns a small fund into a franchise.

Then the dot-com mania arrived, and research stopped getting graded. Robertson deliberately kept Tiger light on tech, convinced the run-up was a bubble. From August 1998 on, value investing fell out of fashion and Tiger lagged badly. A huge stake in US Airways went sour, a bet on the Japanese yen backfired, and investors pulled about $7.7 billion. In his farewell letter, he argued that momentum and speculation had shoved earnings and valuations into the back seat, and that he had no edge in guessing when sanity would return.

Here's the twist: he was basically right, just early. The bubble he refused to ride soon burst. But instead of burning clients' capital to prove a point, Robertson did something rare for a Wall Street legend. He admitted he couldn't read the room and walked away. In a business where the scoreboard updates every second, saying out loud that you can't read the game takes a rare kind of nerve. Being correct eventually is cold comfort when your investors are paying for the wait. Plenty of managers double down when the market stops agreeing with them; Robertson refused to keep playing a changed game with other people's money.

His bigger legacy may be the people he trained. The so-called Tiger Cubs, including Stephen Mandel of Lone Pine, Lee Ainslie of Maverick and Chase Coleman, went on to build some of the biggest hedge funds around, often with Robertson's backing. He also gave away more than $2 billion and signed the Giving Pledge before dying in August 2022 at 90.

quote.text: A market which I frankly do not understand.
quote.src: Julian Robertson, letter to Tiger Management investors, March 30, 2000

takeaways: AI jitters echo 1999: when a market stops making sense, shrinking exposure is allowed.
With the 10-year near 5%, earnings and price matter again.
Oil above $100, a possible December hike: size bets for being early.
